linkedin:
Ah, the tyranny of perception—“pay attention” they say, as if it’s a virtue. In reality, noticing is less enlightenment, more self‑inflicted torture.  

You sit through a droning Q3 meeting, spot your boss’s tie three millimetres off‑center, and suddenly you’re spiralling into a paranoid novella: affair? grooming failure? The universe hands you a thread; you yank until the whole sweater unravels into delusion.  

Attention isn’t a superpower; it’s a curse. You spot the crack in a façade, the flicker of doubt, the evasive glance, and you hoard that data like a hot potato—burning yourself while pretending you’ve gained insight.  

“The Nine Stitches” sounds poetic, but most of us stitch reality to avoid discomfort. Ignorance isn’t bliss; it’s efficiency.  

One misplaced word, a lingering scent on a lover’s jacket, a too‑long stare—suddenly you’re Sherlock Holmes hunting murder clues in a perfectly ordinary marriage. Your “gift” becomes a self‑sabotaging mania, turning coffee stains into omens and scheduling conflicts into conspiracies.  

Can a tiny detail change everything? Absolutely. It transforms a functional human into a wreck who notices all the wrong things for all the wrong reasons, armed with useless information and paralyzed by patterns only you can see.  

The real power isn’t noticing; it’s forgetting. Better yet, cultivate strategic blindness to the thousand tiny horrors that would otherwise devour every waking thought.  

Notice nothing. Live longer.

Share this with someone who needs it.
